Second, Thailand is deeply concerned by the rapid rise of online scam and cyber-enabled fraud, which have evolved into serious transnational organized crimes affecting societies, economies, and human security worldwide. Criminal networks increasingly exploit digital platforms, emerging technologies, and cross-border operational structures to target victims on an unprecedented scale. Thailand recognizes that no state can address these threats alone. We therefore underscore the significance of strengthened international cooperation, timely information sharing, mutual legal assistance, financial investigations, asset recovery, and coordinated law enforcement responses. Enhancing digital literacy and public awareness to prevent victimization, particularly among vulnerable populations, is equally crucial. We appreciate the Member States that joined the adoption of the Bangkok Joint Statement by the Global Partnership Against Online Scams, which was the outcome document of the International Conference on the Global Partnership Against Online Scams on December 25 in Bangkok. Regarding the prevention and suppression of online scams and cyber-enabled fraud in the international scheme, Thailand participated the signing of the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime in Hanoi, Vietnam last year and is currently undertaking the necessary domestic procedures to become a party to the Convention at the earliest opportunity. Mr. Chair, lastly, Thailand further wishes to highlight the importance of early prosecutorial involvement in complex criminal cases. particularly those involving transnational organized crimes, cybercrime corruption, financial crimes, and trafficking related offenses. In increasingly sophisticated and technology driven criminal environments, integrated collaboration between investigators and prosecutors from the earliest stage of a case is essential. Hence, Thailand has continued to strengthen multidisciplinary approaches and institutional coordination among prosecutors, law enforcement authorities, financial intelligence units, and digital forensic experts. We believe that building capacity and promoting practical cooperation among criminal justice actors are critical to ensuring accountability and the effective administration of justice. Mr. Chair, Thailand remains firmly committed to constructive engagement within this Commission and to advancing practical, inclusive, and forward-looking solutions to emerging crime challenges. As we are submitting the candidature for the next term of CCPCJ membership for 2028 to 2030, we stand ready to work with all member states and partners to strengthen criminal justice systems that are effective, humane, resilient and responsive to the needs of our people. Thank you.
Thank you for the statement. I now invite Mr. Dmitry Lubinsky, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation, to address the Commission, Excellency. You have the floor.

Mr. Chairperson. At the outset, let me congratulate you and the other members of the board on your election, and we hope that under your leadership this session will reach its goals and will be marked by practical achievements in efforts to counter transnational organised crime. We are ready to do all we can to contribute to this. The Russian Federation firmly believes that a priority area for the Commission's work should be consistent efforts to step up our common to combat all types of criminal challenges and threats. Very important here is that this work take place with the central coordinating role of the United Nations and in strict accordance with the fundamental principles of international law. As a responsible member of the international community, Russia remains open for constructive dialogue to resolve global tasks related to ending suppressing organised crime in all forms and manifestations. In this context, we again make a call on members to focus on working for effective means to suppress crime, such as by strengthening international legal frameworks and by ensuring anti crime, corruption and a spirit of equality and mutual respect. Unfortunately, we do see a high degree of politicisation of international cooperation in this area too. A number of countries are using various pretexts or even no explanation to refuse to satisfy Russia's requests to provide mutual legal assistance on criminal cases and extradition cases. What's more, there are attempts to introduce political elements to the work of the relevant mechanisms, including Interpol. Mr. Chair, we welcome the signing in Hanoi of the Convention on Cybercrime, which was elaborated on based on an initiative from the Russian Federation. And we call on those states who have not yet signed it to join this very useful, important international legal instrument, and to those who have already signed it to bring it into force and ratify it. The Russian Federation is focused on continuing the expansion of this document's scope with the protocol on additional criminal offences here. Particular attention should go on combating the use of ICT for terrorist and extremist purposes and to prevent drugs trafficking, firearms trafficking and also to take action on crimes using artificial intelligence. The Russian delegation will present a more detailed report here at the session on the implementation and ratification of the Convention on Cybercrime. And we also invite you to come to Russia's event on 3 June, a round table which will discuss the preparations of the protocol on additional offences. Mr. Chairperson, Russia over many years now has been working with UNODC to provide assistance to countries, and this is based on the principles of mutual respect and does not have any political undertone. In particular, in 2025, we increased to $3 million our annual contribution to the UNODC and this money has been earmarked for specialized projects to combat the use of ICT for criminal purposes and also to combat illicit drugs trafficking, corruption, piracy at sea. and we will continue to expand the geographical scope and the amount of this assistance and provide all round operational support. Mr. Chair, once again, let me reiterate the Russian Federation's commitment to combating crime and to, with the Commission, implementing the agenda. Thank you for your attention. And I would also, in conclusion, like to congratulate Ms. Dzhuma on the beginning of her important new mission here in Vienna at this, in this high post. Thank you.

Thank you. Thank you for this statement and I invite now her excellency, his excellency Mr. Kennedy Obed Reyes Lasso, ambassador and permanent representative of El Salvador to address the commission. Floor is yours.

Mr. Chairperson, on behalf of the Government of El Salvador, we congratulate you on your election to chair the work of this Commission, and we also congratulate the members of the Board and thank the Secretariat for all of its work to prepare this session. We also take this opportunity to congratulate Ms. Monica Juma on her appointment as the Director General of UNOV and the Executive Director of UNODC. My country places great importance on this. event and in this respect we reiterate our firm commitment to full respect of the rule of law and provision of justice as the foundations that guarantee equality access and effectively protect our citizens. Mr. Chair, for many years my country faced serious challenges stemming from criminal violence and the actions of terrorist groups and the expansion of criminal groups and these threats have greatly affected public security, economic development and social cohesion and for decades plunged El Salvador into impunity and violence and corruption. But we are now carrying out a comprehensive transformation on public security and criminal justice. This is based on regaining control of territory and institution building and effectively protecting our population. And thanks to the implementation of comprehensive security policies and our efforts to build operational capacity for the state and also our firm commitment, the commitment of our president, we have achieved a historic reduction in our homicide rate and also in cases of extortion, arms trafficking, trafficking in persons and crime in general. El Salvador is modernizing its public institutions and ensuring effective provision of justice and is restructuring its justice system in order to provide our population with safety, security and opportunities. The transformation in our country is reflected in figures. A decade ago, our country was the most violent country in the world, but in 2025, we had a homicide rate of only 1.3 homicides for each 100,000 people. And this rate continues to come down every year. Our national public safety policy, the policy of Nayib Bukele's government, has transformed El Salvador into the safest country in the Western Hemisphere. And these are sustained long-term results. And this thanks to the work we are carrying out in crime prevention, rebuilding the social fabric, and investing more in education and health. Mr. Chair, El Salvador recognizes that transnational organized crime remains a serious global threat and this requires coordinated, effective responses and international cooperation. My country's experience also shows that with bold leadership and with political will, we can make a difference. El Salvador today is a reference. We have useful experience that we could share. And so we stress the importance of information exchanges and of technical assistance and legal cooperation and multilateral mechanisms to combat all types of crime, especially organized crime. We therefore believe it essential to promote a holistic crime prevention strategies that give priority to social inclusion, education and opportunities for young people and that strengthen our communities. El Salvador will continue to work constructively and responsibly with members to advance towards safer, fairer, more humane societies. Thank you.

Thank you. And Excellencies, dear delegates, we will have two more speakers in this morning's sessions because we started with a delay in the morning. And it's now my pleasure to invite Mr. Muhammed Mirat Sabagoliev, Deputy General Prosecutor of Turkmenistan. Sir, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chairperson, distinguished delegates. Turkmenistan is grateful to UNODC for the efforts that went into organizing this important meeting. Our approach to crime prevention is based on the rule of law, effective criminal justice measures, and crime prevention policies. While prosecution of criminals is the most important function of the criminal justice system, Turkmenistan attaches greater importance to crime prevention. Our priority focus is therefore on outreach efforts targeting the population, promoting a culture of lawfulness and supporting social policies aimed at eliminating the root causes of crime. In practice, this means combating trafficking in persons and corruption. under the coordination of the general prosecutor's office. We actively contribute to the work of the regional body of the Financial Action Task Force, the Eurasian Group, and other bodies aimed at that work on countering money laundering and terrorist financing, including the Globe Network and the International Anti-Corruption Academy. Thank you for this statement. And now I have the pleasure to invite Mrs. Christine Klein, Director of International Negotiations, International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Bureau of the Department of State of the United States of America. Madam, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. At the outset, the United States congratulates Dr. Monica Juma on her appointment to lead UNODC. Chair, the United States is here to sound the alarm on a crisis claiming the lives of children in our country and around the world: transnational sextortion. Sextortion is the fastest growing crime against American children. With permission of the families, let me be clear about the cost. Braden Michael Bone from Wisconsin was 15 years old. Caleb Moore from Kansas was 14 years old. Evan James Bettler from Missouri was 16 years old. James Woods from Ohio was 17 years old. Jordan Demay from Michigan was 17 years old. Riley Bassford from New York was 15 years old. Ryan Charles Last from California was 17 years old. Timothy Barnett from South Carolina was 13 years old. Walker Montgomery from Mississippi was 16 years old. These are among the 41 American children who have died by suicide since 2021 as a direct result of sextortion schemes. 41 children, 41 families destroyed. These stories should break the hearts of everyone in this room. Families shattered, communities grieving, futures stolen. We know how this works. Sextortion offenders pose as peers or romantic interests on social media or gaming platforms. They gain our children's trust, manipulating them into sharing intimate images, then threaten to release them or AI generated forgeries unless the child provides more explicit content or pays up. In the most sadistic cases, these predators go further, coercing children to harm themselves or others, perpetrating extreme and degrading abuse. The numbers are adding up. In 2022, 10,000 US reports of transnational sextortion. In 2023, 28,000. In 2024, 36,000. In 2025, more than 50,000. Most of these schemes originate in Nigeria, Cote d'Ivoire, and the Philippines. Unfortunately, governments are not doing enough. In Nigeria, scammers have been sentenced to prison terms with the option of paying a fine instead. To be clear, criminals can avoid prison for defrauding Americans by paying as little as $200. This is unacceptable. Governments must act. But the private sector also has a critical role to play in preventing their platforms from being misused to harm children online. They can incorporate safety by design, including through ensuring default protective measures and settings that safeguard children and children's information, and should provide more timely and robust reporting to law enforcement of apparent online child sexual exploitation. The United States is taking action. In March, President Trump signed an executive order on combating cybercrime fraud and predatory schemes against Americans to counter attacks on our citizens, to support victims, and specifically call for action related to sextortion schemes. The United States will not wait. We will deploy every tool in our arsenal, sanctions, visa restrictions, prosecutions, extraditions and more to dismantle these networks and protect our citizens. This week, we tabled the first UN resolution calling for greater action against transnational sextortion of children. We urge every government here to match our resolve, sponsor this resolution, and implement it. You must hold criminals accountable and deliver real protection for our children. As we leave this hall, I ask you to remember not only the numbers of those impacted, but the names behind them. Brayden, Caleb, Evan, James, Jordan, Riley, Ryan, Timothy, Walker. Their lives were cut short. Their families carry grief that will never fade. Let us honor them by committing to action today so that no child, no parent, no community has to endure this tragedy again. Thank you.
